### Purpose Statement

This guidance compares Netskope's ZTNA vs. Universal ZTNA approaches, evaluating their impacts on network security roadmaps and providing strategic direction for zero trust network access implementation.

### Introduction

Netskope's Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solution (often delivered via *Netskope Private Access*) is a modern VPN-replacement focused on secure, identity-based application access for remote users. Universal ZTNA (UZTNA) is Netskope's next-generation approach that extends zero-trust access beyond remote users to encompass on-premises access, branch offices, and even unmanaged IoT/OT devices. In essence, UZTNA broadens the scope of ZTNA and converges networking and security functions into a unified framework
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). UZTNA represents the logical next step in the Zero Trust journey for Gainwell, but carries with it the need to reconsider impacted network and network security strategies.

## Problem

Current technology roadmaps being planned for network, network defense, and endpoint, are not factoring in the potential impact of advancing zero trust capabilities in their domains, and as a result, are moving in potentially adverse directions.

## Scope

To illuminate how specific improvements in our Zero Trust Network Access design could impact related technology domains, this report first contrasts Netskope's ZTNA and Universal ZTNA in terms of architecture, capabilities, and deployment models. It then analyzes how moving from ZTNA to Universal ZTNA affects an enterprise's network and security roadmap -- specifically examining changes to SD-WAN requirements, Network Access Control (NAC) (e.g. Cisco ISE), and perimeter defense strategy. It further highlight shifts in operational complexity, policy enforcement, and integration with existing infrastructure, using tables and key points for clarity.

## Netskope ZTNA vs. Universal ZTNA: Architecture, Capabilities, Deployment

**Netskope ZTNA (Traditional):** Netskope's standard ZTNA (often referred to as Netskope Private Access) provides zero-trust application-level access primarily for remote users. Its architecture typically involves a cloud-based trust broker and application connectors (publishers) deployed in front of private apps (in data centers or cloud)
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). Users run a Netskope client (or use clientless browser access for web apps) on managed devices, which authenticates their identity and device posture to the cloud broker. Once verified, the broker tunnels user traffic to the appropriate app connector, granting least-privilege access only to the authorized application -- not the full network
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). This hides apps from direct exposure and prevents lateral movement, much like other ZTNA solutions. However, traditional ZTNA was designed mainly for remote access. Users on the internal network typically did not go through the ZTNA path -- their access was governed by LAN security (e.g., NAC) and internal firewalls instead. Likewise, unmanaged devices and IoT/OT machines were out of ZTNA's scope.

**Netskope Universal ZTNA:** UZTNA is an expanded architecture delivered as part of the Netskope One SASE platform. It extends zero-trust access to any user or device, in any location
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). Architecturally, it combines Netskope Private Access with new components like Netskope One Converged Gateway and Netskope Device Intelligence:

- **Converged Cloud + Edge Enforcement:** In addition to the cloud-based broker, Universal ZTNA can leverage on-premises Netskope One Gateways (physical/virtual appliances at branches or data centers) as local enforcement points
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access)\[\[2\]\>](<https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway>). This means zero-trust brokers exist both in the cloud and on local networks, working together. For example, an enterprise can host the ZTNA "publisher" service directly on a branch gateway appliance. This localizes traffic for on-site users (avoiding hairpinning to cloud) while still enforcing zero-trust policies. It delivers a *consistent user experience everywhere* (remote or on-prem) since policies apply uniformly and performance is optimized locally when possible
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>).

- **Device Intelligence & Agentless Options:** UZTNA introduces context-aware device intelligence to discover and secure devices that cannot run an agent, such as IoT and OT endpoints. The Netskope Device Intelligence service automatically classifies devices, assesses their risk posture via network telemetry (e.g. using the 5G/SD-WAN gateway), and informs access policy. This effectively brings non-user devices into the zero-trust framework. Agent-based or agentless access is supported: managed PCs can use the Netskope client as before, while unmanaged BYOD or third-party devices might use clientless web portals or network-based identification
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). By contrast, traditional ZTNA was mostly agent-based and had limited visibility into headless devices
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>).

- **Integrated Security Services:** Universal ZTNA converges with Netskope's broader Security Service Edge capabilities. It has built-in threat protection and data loss prevention (DLP) inspection for private application traffic on both remote and local connections. In other words, when users connect to an internal app via UZTNA, the traffic can be scanned by Netskope's threat intelligence and DLP engines (the same engines used for CASB/SWG), applying consistent security controls. Traditional Netskope ZTNA primarily focused on access control and might not natively inspect payloads for threats/data -- any deep inspection was left to separate tools or not done at all. UZTNA's embedded inspection means zero-trust access and security filtering are unified in one step.

- **Continuous Risk Assessment:** In UZTNA, access decisions are continuously risk-adjusted. Netskope's Zero Trust Engine shares real-time context about user behavior, device state, and threats to adapt permissions on the fly
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). For instance, if a device becomes high-risk or behaving abnormally, UZTNA can restrict its access immediately (dynamic policy). Earlier ZTNA solutions generally granted access after an initial check (authentication & posture at login) and did not change permissions until the next session
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). UZTNA's AI-driven policy optimization (via Netskope "Copilot") further automates fine-grained policy creation and adjustments based on observed traffic patterns -- reducing admins' workload while tightening security.

- **Unified Management:** Universal ZTNA is managed through a single console as part of the Netskope One platform, which also manages CASB, SWG, and SD-WAN components. Policies for all users and devices -- whether remote or on-campus -- are defined in one place
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). In contrast, a traditional setup might involve multiple management points: one for ZTNA, another for NAC (for on-site users), and perhaps others for VPN or endpoint management
\[\[3\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer>). UZTNA's unified policy engine ensures that the same access rules and zero-trust principles apply everywhere, simplifying operations and eliminating policy silos
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>).

The table below summarizes key differences between Netskope's standard ZTNA and Universal ZTNA across architecture, capabilities, and deployment:

| Aspect | Netskope ZTNA (Traditional) | Netskope Universal ZTNA |
|--------|------------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Primary Use Case** | Remote user access to private apps (VPN replacement) [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). On-prem users typically handled via traditional LAN security (not through ZTNA). | All users (remote, branch, on-campus) *and* devices (including IoT/OT) under zero-trust access [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). Consistent enforcement regardless of location or device type. |
| **Supported Devices** | Managed user devices only. Requires Netskope client (agent) or browser for access. IoT/OT not addressed. | Managed & unmanaged devices. Supports agent-based *and* agentless access [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). Includes non-user devices (IoT/OT) via device discovery and posture profiling. |
| **Architecture & Enforcement** | Cloud broker + app connectors. Cloud-based trust broker mediates user-to-app connections; requires connector (publisher) near each app/DC [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). No on-prem ZTNA enforcement for LAN traffic; relies on existing NAC/firewalls. | Cloud + on-prem gateway brokers. Cloud-native broker integrated with optional Netskope One Gateway appliances at branches/DCs [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). Enables local Zero Trust enforcement on LAN (east-west) and cloud-based enforcement for remote (north-south). |
| **Policy Engine** | Separate policy silos: ZTNA policies mainly for remote access; on-site access governed by NAC policies separately. Limited context-sharing between solutions. | Single unified policy engine for all access scenarios [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). Zero Trust rules consistently applied to remote and local sessions. Real-time risk scoring influences policy (adaptive authZ) [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). One management console for configuration [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). |
| **Security Services** | Focus on access control (identity & device-check at login). Little or no built-in traffic inspection for threats or sensitive data -- would require additional SWG/DLP tools outside the ZTNA channel. | Integrated threat & data protection. Private app traffic is inspected in-line by Netskope's threat prevention and DLP engines, even for on-prem users. Provides consistent malware and data leak protection as part of the access session. |
| **Adaptability** | Static once connected. Access is granted per session; changes in user/device risk during a session are not accounted for until re-authentication [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). | Continuous verification. Access can adjust dynamically based on live risk signals (user behavior analytics, device posture changes) [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). Also leverages AI (Copilot) to auto-tune policies over time. |
| **Deployment Model** | Delivered as a cloud service (Security Service Edge). Requires lightweight connectors in each private app environment and an endpoint client. Branches use existing routers/VPN for connectivity; ZTNA kicks in mainly for remote/off-net users. | Offered as part of a converged SASE solution. Flexible deployment: can be deployed at branch/edge (as a physical/virtual appliance running Netskope One Gateway) and/or consumed via cloud [\[2\]](https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway). Built to replace or integrate with branch SD-WAN devices and campus NAC infrastructure. |

Citations: The above comparison is supported by Netskope's documentation and press releases. For instance, UZTNA is explicitly described as extending access to *"remote, branch, campus, and non-user devices (IoT/OT)"* with unified policies
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>), whereas traditional ZTNA was "designed mainly for remote user access"
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>). UZTNA supports agentless access and local broker capabilities
\[\[1\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access>), whereas earlier ZTNA was predominantly agent-based. UZTNA's integration of threat/DLP engines and device intelligence for IoT is noted in announcements. The unified single-console approach and replacement of legacy VPN/NAC/VDI by UZTNA are also emphasized by Netskope
[\[1\]\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access).

## Impact of Transitioning from ZTNA to Universal ZTNA on Network & Security Roadmaps

Adopting Universal ZTNA is not just a feature upgrade -- it has strategic implications for an enterprise's network and security architecture. Migrating from a traditional ZTNA (plus existing NAC/VPN infrastructure) to UZTNA will influence how we design branch connectivity, campus access controls, and perimeter defenses. Below, let us analyze three key areas of impact and highlight changes in operational complexity, policy enforcement, and integration needs.

## 1. SD-WAN and Network Architecture Implications

**Traditional Setup:** With standard ZTNA, organizations still relied on their existing network topology for on-premise access and site connectivity. Typically, an SD-WAN solution (or traditional WAN) connected branch offices and data centers for internal traffic, while internet-bound traffic might go through centralized egress or local breakouts with security stack. Remote users used ZTNA (or VPN) to come into the network. This meant networking (SD-WAN) and security (ZTNA, plus firewall/IDS) were separate domains -- often managed through different consoles. The SD-WAN optimized network performance, but had limited awareness of user/application identity or security posture
\[\[3\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer>). Likewise, ZTNA ensured secure access for remote users, but on-site users' traffic typically bypassed it and was controlled by NAC and internal firewalls.

**With Universal ZTNA:** The network and security functions become more converged. UZTNA is delivered via Netskope's SASE platform that integrates SD-WAN capabilities with zero-trust enforcement. For example, Netskope's Converged Gateway provides secure SD-WAN features (dynamic path selection, routing, WAN optimization) combined with SSE security at the edge
\[\[2\]\]\[\[2\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway>). As a result, future network designs can simplify or alter SD-WAN requirements in several ways:

- Integrated SD-WAN + Security: Instead of backhauling ZTNA traffic over an existing SD-WAN, organizations can deploy Netskope's edge gateway at branches which *combines routing and zero-trust broker functions*. This yields a "one-box" solution at branch offices that handles local traffic breakout, steering authorized flows to applications (cloud or data center) with zero trust checks in-line
\[\[2\]\]\[\[2\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway>). The Zero Trust Engine shares context with the SD-WAN function, enabling application-aware QoS and path selection based on user/app risk and priority \[\[2\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway>). Policy enforcement becomes uniform -- the same gateway enforces security policy and network policy, reducing the chance of mismatches. For the network team, this may mean evaluating Netskope's SD-WAN features versus your existing SD-WAN: some enterprises may gradually replace standalone SD-WAN appliances at branches with Netskope's converged gateway to streamline operations
\[\[2\]\]\[\[2\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway>). Others might integrate by connecting their current SD-WAN fabric to Netskope's cloud services (for example, establishing clean hand-offs for cloud-app traffic).

- Direct-to-App Connectivity: UZTNA encourages a direct connectivity model. Remote and branch users connect straight to the application via the optimal path (internet or hybrid cloud), authenticated by the nearest broker (cloud or on-prem). This reduces dependency on hub-and-spoke MPLS or VPN tunnels. SD-WAN configurations may shift to favor local internet breakouts, since security is assured by UZTNA on those paths. The role of the data center as a traffic hub diminishes, impacting network design. For instance, branch offices might no longer need to tunnel all traffic to HQ for security inspection; they can route traffic directly to Netskope's cloud or to other branches securely. This can alter bandwidth planning -- potentially less MPLS/backhaul traffic and more internet traffic at branches. Network teams should ensure branch internet links are robust, and possibly leverage Netskope's built-in 4G/5G options (e.g., *Zero Trust SIM*) for backup connectivity
\[\[3\]\]\[\[3\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer>).

- Context-Aware Path Optimization: Because Universal ZTNA shares identity, device posture, and application context with the networking plane, routing decisions can be smarter. For example, critical app traffic for an authenticated user might get priority and optimal path selection across the SD-WAN, whereas unknown or unauthorized traffic is dropped or deprioritized at the edge
\[\[3\]\]\[\[3\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer>). This tight integration means SD-WAN policy and security policy merge, simplifying policy management. Previously, network engineers managed QoS and routing in one system and security in another; now, UZTNA's unified console can coordinate both (e.g. apply network segmentation or QoS based on zero-trust categories like device risk).

- Operational & Integration Impact: Transitioning to this model can reduce complexity in the long term, but requires careful integration in the short term. On one hand, having one converged platform for SD-WAN and security means fewer devices and consoles to manage, and eliminates a lot of manual alignment between network and security configurations
\[\[3\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer)\[\[2\]\>](<https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway>). Troubleshooting can improve with end-to-end visibility (Netskope's Digital Experience Monitoring can trace performance across the LAN, WAN, and cloud)
\[\[3\]\](<https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer>). On the other hand, adopting UZTNA might mean replacing or upgrading branch equipment, retraining staff on new SASE systems, and possibly running Netskope in parallel with an existing SD-WAN during a migration phase. If an organization uses a Cisco SD-WAN or similar, they might initially integrate by forwarding traffic from branch routers to Netskope's nearest point of presence for policy enforcement, then gradually weigh if Netskope's SD-WAN features can supplant the legacy solution.

In summary, SD-WAN requirements will evolve from a standalone network concern to part of a holistic secure access design. Expect a roadmap that includes providing reliable local internet access at all sites, deploying Netskope gateway appliances or virtual devices in strategic locations, and ensuring your SD-WAN (if retained) can route intelligently into the Netskope environment. The end-state is a more simplified network architecture with unified security and network policy -- aligning with the SASE vision of minimum separate components
[\[2\]\[2\]](https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway).

## 2. Impact on Network Access Control (Cisco ISE and NAC Solutions)

**Traditional Setup:** In current enterprise networks, Network Access Control (NAC) systems like *Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE)* are used to enforce security on the internal network. NAC typically authenticates devices when they connect (via 802.1X, agent, or captive portal), checks compliance (posture, certificates), and then assigns the device to an appropriate VLAN or access role. Cisco ISE might, for example, put a corporate laptop on a trusted network segment after successful authentication, or put a guest/unknown device in a restricted VLAN. NAC can also do limited device profiling (identifying device types) and trigger network-based segmentation. However, NAC has limitations in today's environment: once a device is allowed on the network, it often gains broad L3 access internally, since NAC isn't application-aware. As noted in a Netskope analysis, *"Traditional NAC grants broad network access after authentication instead of enforcing application-specific restrictions... and doesn't monitor behavior after granting initial access"*, leading to potential blind spots [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). NAC also struggles with IoT/OT devices that can't easily authenticate or run agents -- often leading to ad-hoc MAC address whitelisting that is prone to spoofing [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). In a hybrid work scenario, enterprises end up maintaining separate access control mechanisms: NAC for on-prem users and devices, and ZTNA/VPN for remote users, each with their own policies and consoles [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer).

**With Universal ZTNA:** UZTNA can subsume many NAC functions into the zero-trust framework, fundamentally changing how we secure internal networks. Netskope's UZTNA is explicitly positioned to *"replace legacy NAC"* approaches with a more dynamic solution [\[2\]](https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway)[\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access).
Key changes include:

- Unified Access Control (Remote and Local): With UZTNA, the same zero-trust principles apply when a user or device is in the office as when they are remote. Instead of granting a device full network access once on LAN, UZTNA would require the device (or user on that device) to authenticate continuously for each application. In practice, a user in the office would still run the Netskope client (or be identified via an agentless mechanism on the LAN), and when they try to reach an internal application, the request goes through the UZTNA broker which checks policy and posture just like it would for a remote user [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). The internal network thus becomes an untrusted zone -- simply plugging in an approved device to a switch port is not enough to reach internal apps. This reduces reliance on VLAN segmentation because the real access decisions happen at the application layer via UZTNA. Cisco ISE's role can shift to a lighter one: e.g. still performing initial authentication to allow network connectivity (EAP-TLS, etc.), but not authorizing access to specific resources -- that's handled by UZTNA policy. In some cases, organizations might even choose to bypass heavy NAC enforcement; for instance, using a simple dynamic guest network for unknown devices and letting Netskope's Device Intelligence assess and control their activity at a higher layer.

- Device Posture and Profiling: UZTNA's device intelligence can automatically discover devices on the network and determine their type and risk (using AI/ML on network metadata) [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). This overlaps with (and arguably exceeds) the device profiling capabilities of Cisco ISE. For example, instead of ISE's static profiling based on MAC OUI or DHCP fingerprint, Netskope can classify an IoT device and even detect anomalous behavior (like an IP camera sending SSH traffic unexpectedly) [\[3\]\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). UZTNA can then dynamically respond -- e.g. isolate or micro-segment that device. In fact, Netskope notes an example where a camera's risk score jumping triggers a *"policy update to dynamically microsegment the device across existing switches and APs"* [\[3\]\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). This implies UZTNA can integrate with the LAN infrastructure (possibly via APIs or SD-LAN integrations) to quarantine a device, much as a NAC solution would -- but triggered by more advanced analytics. In roadmap terms, this suggests that Cisco ISE (or any NAC) could be gradually phased down; the heavy lifting of device compliance and segmentation can be offloaded to UZTNA's smarter policy engine.

- Consolidated Policy and Visibility: Instead of maintaining parallel sets of access rules (one in ISE for on-prem, one in ZTNA for remote), an organization can move toward one central zero-trust policy. UZTNA provides consistent authentication, authorization and logging for all access attempts, whether coming from inside or outside the network [\[3\]\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). This means security teams get a single view of application access events. Also, any data protection controls (DLP) or threat policies apply uniformly -- something NAC by itself never did. As Netskope puts it, *"local network users benefit from the same advanced security that remote user traffic gets when passing through the Netskope platform"* [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer). For example, if a user on the LAN tries to download sensitive data from an internal app, the DLP policy can catch it through UZTNA inspection, whereas previously that might go unnoticed by ISE (which doesn't inspect content).

**Changes for Cisco ISE:** Cisco ISE is a powerful and widely-used NAC. Moving to UZTNA doesn't necessarily mean an overnight elimination of ISE -- but its role will change. In early phases, ISE can be integrated with UZTNA: Netskope's device intelligence can feed data into ISE or vice-versa. Indeed, Netskope indicates UZTNA's device intelligence *"extends remediation and access control to the east-west plane through integrations with leading third-party NAC vendors"*. This suggests that, for example, Netskope could signal ISE to place a device in a quarantine VLAN if its risk is high. Over time, as confidence in UZTNA grows, enterprises might choose to retire complex NAC policies. The roadmap might involve relaxing some ISE enforcement (to reduce redundancy and complexity) and letting UZTNA policies dictate access. Eventually, some organizations may decide that ISE is only needed for basic network onboarding (802.1X authentication to ensure the user/device is known) -- after which UZTNA controls everything the device can do. Other capabilities of ISE like guest management or NAC for non-IP devices might still be relevant, but those too could potentially be handled by alternative means (e.g., Netskope could manage guest access via clientless portal). In summary, Universal ZTNA allows NAC consolidation: fewer SSIDs/VLANs, fewer ACLs on switches, and more reliance on an identity-centric overlay. This simplifies operations by removing one layer of policy duplication [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer), and helps avoid the scenario of "inconsistent policies across multiple consoles" that organizations previously faced with separate NAC and remote access systems [\[3\]](https://www.netskope.com/blog/legacy-nac-cant-keep-up-uztna-is-the-answer).

**Operational Complexity:** Reducing dependence on NAC can streamline IT operations significantly. NAC solutions like ISE are notoriously complex to maintain (certificate management, profiling databases, etc.), and any policy change often requires coordination with network teams. With UZTNA, many of those controls move into a cloud-managed policy, reducing on-prem infrastructure. However, admins will need to ensure integration with identity providers (e.g., Active Directory or cloud IdP) so that UZTNA has the necessary user directory info -- similar to what ISE needed. Also, careful planning is needed to migrate gradually: perhaps start by using UZTNA for new use cases (like contractor access or IoT segmentation) and slowly back off ISE for those, before fully switching on-campus user device control to UZTNA. During transition, coexistence is possible -- e.g., use ISE to do an initial posture check and then use Netskope for app access enforcement. From a policy enforcement perspective, the change should tighten security: instead of granting a device broad network trust after NAC check, UZTNA's continuous verification ensures least-privilege always. The upside is a reduced attack surface (even an internal threat or compromised device can't scan the whole network because it has no network-layer access). The potential downside is if the UZTNA client or integration fails, users might have trouble accessing resources even on-site -- thus high availability and good network connectivity to Netskope's cloud/gateway become critical parts of the roadmap planning.

## 3. Perimeter Defense and Security Architecture Impacts

**Traditional Setup:** In legacy network designs, a lot of focus is on the network perimeter -- typically guarded by next-gen firewalls, intrusion prevention systems, and VPN gateways at the edge of corporate data centers. Remote access was funneled through DMZ-hosted solutions (VPN concentrators or ZTNA cloud connectors coming into a defined point). Internal applications were often partially exposed in a DMZ or through port forwarding for remote access. The perimeter defense strategy included maintaining hardened external boundaries, while internal networks were relatively flat or segmented by VLANs and internal firewalls. With initial ZTNA adoption, some of this changed (for example, fewer VPN appliances needed if ZTNA is cloud-based, and internal apps hidden behind ZTNA publishers, not exposed at the perimeter). However, traditional ZTNA typically did *not* eliminate the need for a perimeter firewall -- enterprises still kept firewalls to filter outbound internet access and to protect internal networks from external threats.

**With Universal ZTNA:** The concept of a singular "perimeter" further blurs. Security enforcement becomes more distributed across cloud and on-prem nodes, and is tied to identity and device posture rather than purely IP addresses or physical location. Key impacts on perimeter strategy:

- Reduction of Exposed Services: With a full UZTNA approach, organizations can ensure that no internal applications are directly exposed to the internet at all -- not even through VPN endpoints. The UZTNA cloud broker or gateway is the only entry point, and it does not permit any traffic until authenticated. This means things like VPN concentrators, or public-facing remote desktop gateways, can be decommissioned. The attack surface at the network edge shrinks further. For example, previously you might have a Cisco ASA or similar appliance listening on certain ports for VPN -- under UZTNA you might rely entirely on Netskope's cloud service (with its robust globally distributed infrastructure) to handle remote connections. The roadmap should plan for the retirement of legacy remote access infrastructure (VPN appliances, legacy VDI jump boxes if they were mainly for remote access) to streamline the perimeter.

- Distributed Firewalling: Universal ZTNA leverages Netskope's cloud and on-prem gateway as zero trust enforcement points for both north-south and east-west traffic. In effect, Netskope's solution brings firewall-like capabilities closer to the user/device. For north-south (user-to-app) traffic, the SSE platform can do policy-based allow/deny, threat inspection, URL filtering, etc., as traffic goes to private apps or the internet. For east-west (within a site) the on-prem Netskope gateway can enforce micro-segmentation rules. This potentially reduces the load on central firewalls. For instance, rather than hairpinning branch traffic to a central firewall for inter-VLAN filtering, a Netskope branch gateway could enforce those rules locally. Over time, an enterprise could simplify perimeter firewall rules because fewer sessions actually hit the traditional firewall. Policy enforcement is largely handled by the zero-trust layer. The perimeter firewall might transition to a "backstop" role -- allowing Netskope connectors/brokers to talk through, and handling any residual generic traffic not yet on the ZTNA framework.

- Consistent Policy Inside and Out: Historically, companies had strict policies at the internet gateway (e.g. web filtering, intrusion detection for inbound traffic) but internally, once traffic was inside, monitoring was lighter. UZTNA changes that by applying similar inspection and access rules everywhere. The perimeter strategy thus shifts from just "protect the boundary" to "assume no boundary." Each user/device interaction with an app is checked as if it were crossing a secure boundary, regardless of origin. This will likely reduce the emphasis on internal network firewall projects (like segmenting every internal subnet with ACLs) because the zero-trust approach is doing that logically. Instead, the security roadmap might focus on consolidating policy management in the UZTNA/SASE console (so that what used to be firewall ACLs, VPN user profiles, NAC rules, etc., all become part of UZTNA policies). It's a shift toward *policy-based access* over *perimeter-based access*.

- Simplified Edge and Improved Remote Experience: With UZTNA integrated into SASE, remote offices and remote users all connect through Netskope's NewEdge network (global cloud network), which is built for performance and security. This means the perimeter is effectively everywhere the user is, but controlled by Netskope's cloud. Users get a fast local access (through nearest POP or local gateway) rather than tromboning through a distant corporate data center. This can enhance user experience while maintaining security, turning the perimeter from a bottleneck into a distributed fabric. For the security team, less time is spent on maintaining edge hardware (like upgrading firewalls or VPNs); instead they ensure the Netskope connectivity is in place and reliable.

**Policy Enforcement and Integration:** Adopting UZTNA doesn't mean you throw away all firewalls on day one. Integration is key: your existing perimeter firewalls (e.g., Palo Alto, Check Point, etc., or even cloud security groups) will need to be tuned to work with the new model. For instance, if internal apps are now only reachable via the Netskope publisher, you'd configure your firewalls to allow inbound traffic only from Netskope (locking down any other access). Outbound, you might permit branch gateways to talk to Netskope cloud and block other direct Internet paths for sensitive apps, ensuring all traffic goes through the secured channel. Over time, as more traffic goes through Netskope, you could potentially reduce firewall capacity (saving cost) or repurpose them for other uses (like purely as an IDS sensor or for legacy systems that can't use ZTNA). Also, many enterprises integrate Netskope's logs with their SIEM/SOAR just as they did their firewall logs -- that becomes the new central monitoring of "perimeter" activity (which is now distributed user activity).

**Operational Complexity:** From an operations perspective, moving to a UZTNA-centric perimeter strategy can greatly simplify rule management. Instead of juggling firewall rules, VPN user groups, NAC policies, etc., admins define one set of contextual policies (e.g., *"finance app accessible to finance team with corporate devices and up-to-date patches"*, *"IoT sensors can only communicate to IoT gateway service on port X"*, *"no data upload from OT devices"*, etc.). These get enforced by the appropriate component (cloud or on-prem). This reduces complexity and chances for misconfiguration between systems. There is also a reduction in appliance sprawl -- organizations might not need separate appliances for web gateway, remote access, NAC, DLP at the edge, etc.; Netskope's converged solution covers many of those [\[2\]\[2\]](https://www.netskope.com/products/converged-gateway). That said, during the transition, complexity might increase temporarily: running UZTNA while still maintaining the legacy perimeter as backup or in areas not yet migrated means double effort for a period. Clear planning is needed to identify which legacy controls can be turned off as equivalent UZTNA controls come online.

**Overall, the perimeter is reinvented:** it becomes user- and app-centric, not location-centric. Security follows the user/device everywhere via UZTNA. The roadmap impact is a shift to cloud-delivered perimeter services and a zero-trust mindset internally, with less emphasis on traditional network segmentation walls. By moving to Universal ZTNA, enterprises ultimately aim to *"cut complexity, reduce risk, and turn secure access into an enabler, rather than a barrier"*, as Netskope's product team puts it.

## Conclusion

Transitioning to Netskope's Universal ZTNA brings about a more unified and adaptive security architecture. It bridges the gap between networking and security, altering how enterprises plan their infrastructure. SD-WAN solutions must align with a cloud-first, identity-aware approach; NAC solutions like Cisco ISE can be streamlined or even largely replaced by the new model; and the very notion of a network perimeter shifts to a distributed zero-trust fabric. These changes can significantly reduce operational complexity and improve security -- but they require careful planning in the roadmap. Organizations should pilot UZTNA in targeted areas, integrate it with existing systems during a phased migration, and update their policies and teams' skillsets to fully leverage the benefits.

By comparing the traditional ZTNA and Universal ZTNA side-by-side and examining these roadmap implications, enterprises can chart a path forward that modernizes their network security without compromising performance or manageability. Netskope's UZTNA, with its comprehensive approach, provides a compelling opportunity to consolidate tools (VPN, NAC, etc.), enforce consistent zero-trust policies everywhere, and enhance protection for an era of hybrid work and ubiquitous connectivity [\[1\]](https://www.netskope.com/security-defined/what-is-zero-trust-network-access). The end result is a more simplified, scalable, and secure network where policy follows the user and device, not the physical network -- fulfilling the zero trust mantra of *"never trust, always verify"* across the entire enterprise environment.

## Recommended Next Steps

The recent Network / Network Security Summit (Oct. 2025) revealed that, left unaddressed, multiple capabilities roadmaps will progress in directions that diverge from the optimal path if Zero Trust architecture is to be advanced. In order to ensure resources are not committed to unnecessary, and indeed, unhelpful directions, it is advisable that a working session, led by Enterprise Architecture, devoted to evaluating the broader impact of advancing zero trust maturity across network, network security, and endpoints be held.

- Who: Attendees of such a workshop should include thought leaders in the following domains: Networking, Network Access Control, Firewalls, Compliance, and possibly others yet to be determined.

- What: The objective of such a workshop would be to review and revise these disparate roadmaps to ensure better alignment to the overall objectives of improving Gainwell security posture while optimising operational costs.

- Why: Outcomes from this working session would then be used to revise and refactor budgetary and technology plans for the impacted technology delivery domains.

- When: Given the current schedule of events, as well as upcoming holidays, it might be best to plan such an event for soon after the start of the new calendar year.
